en: Preface to the Abridged Explanation of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (The Smaller Sukhāvatī-vyūha), Composed by the Śramaṇa Dayou of Wu Commandery.

Now, the tranquil light of true purity originally possesses no distinction between suffering and joy; yet, as deluded consciousness proliferates in confusion, there subsequently arise the categories of the holy and the ordinary.
Because they differ in that they drift through the five turbidities and fail to pervade the single true reality, our Śākyamuni Buddha manifested birth in this Endurance World (*sahā-lokadhātu*).

At the auspicious assembly in the Jeta Grove, he addressed the keen faculties of Śāriputra, opened the gateway of his vow for the treasury of Dharma, and pointed toward the wondrous land of Sukhāvatī.
Therein, the jade groves and crystal ponds directly manifest the source of the mind; the lifespan and radiance fully reveal one's own nature.

The nature [of Buddhahood] is where all sages dwell together; it is not attained through minor virtues. Maintaining the Name for seven days with an undistracted mind is the principle of the vehicle’s essence.
The source of Buddhahood is identical from the very beginning. Through unconditional compassion, response occurs without deliberation.

Realizing that the fundamental endowment of the mind alone makes even billions of lands not distant, one knows the Great Vow can be relied upon. The three great kalpas are traversed horizontally; the scriptural text is concise.
In accordance with the Buddha’s profound and subtle intent, although I have recited [the scriptures] many times, my detailed study has been meager.
Seeing that the writings of former sages are seldom heard by those of this degenerate age, I have humbly endeavored to circulate them and briefly provide citations.

I pray that all who share these aspirations may universally form pure karmic conditions, realize non-arising, and together ascend to the stage of non-retrogression. Thus it is said. Composed by Dharma Master Ci'en of the Tang Dynasty, for the sake of Amitābha.
The *Tongzan* (General Commentary) consists of one fascicle. Various masters, including Jingjue of Mount Gu and Lingzhi of the Song dynasty, all composed commentaries and records.

Masters Lun Shigu of Siqu and Xin Shi both previously compiled annotated versions. Now, wishing to be concise for the sake of beginners, I have produced this separately, each following its own intent.
A Brief Commentary on the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* Spoken by the Buddha; An Explanation of the Title of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* Spoken by the Buddha.
Regarding the fivefold profound meaning (*pañcavidha-gambhīrārtha*) of this sūtra’s title, following the Master of Gushan, I take those who have attained fruition in the Western Land as...

The name is "Vaipulya" (Extensive), its essence is the True Mark (dharmatā), its principle is faith, aspiration, and pure karma, its function is the relinquishing of suffering and the attainment of bliss, and its pedagogical characteristic is the "fresh butter" Mahāyāna.
First, regarding the explanation of the name: "Spoken by the Buddha" refers to the proclamation by Śākyamuni, the primary teacher, through his four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
In Sanskrit, *Buddha* translates into Chinese as "The Awakened One" (*Jùézhě*), one of the ten titles, signifying ultimate awakening.

To fully comprehend the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is called "perfect awakening" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). To preach with joy means to teach in accordance with the capacities of the listeners, which accords with the Buddha’s compassionate intent.

Furthermore, because this sutra is spoken by the five classes of people in common—distinguishing it from the teachings of bodhisattvas, celestial seers (*ṛṣi*), or manifested beings—it is termed "spoken by the Buddha.
*Amitābha* is translated here as "Immeasurable Life. The *Sūtra* states that the lifespan of that Buddha and...

For immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) kalpas, sentient beings have perceived the lifespan of the Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) through its manifested duration, yet neither devas nor humans can know its measure;
how much less so for the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*) or the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*)? Furthermore, the *Immeasurable Light Sūtra* states:
"The light of that Buddha is immeasurable, illuminating the lands of the ten directions without obstruction. Moreover, "Buddha" is a general title, whereas "Amitābha" is [the specific name].

The title "Śākyamuni" (釋迦) refers to the Teacher of this world; since all sentient beings know him, only his general title is mentioned. The title "Amitābha" (彌陀), however, refers to the Guide of the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
as it is necessary to manifest this specific meaning, his particular title is revealed. As for the word "sūtra" (經): it signifies "Dharma" and "constancy.

It is that which the ten realms of existence alike follow and which remains unchanging throughout the three periods of time. Because it was proclaimed from the golden mouth of the Sage, it is called a sūtra.

"Sūtra" is a general term, while "spoken by the Buddha" and so forth are specific names. There are three kinds of sūtras: namely, those concerning teaching (*śāsana*), practice (*pratipatti*), and principle (*tattva*).

Relying on the teaching to cultivate practice, and through practice to manifest the principle—these are the categories. "Buddha" has the meaning of awakening; because it refers to the perfection of cultivation, it belongs to the category of practice.
"Sūtra" (teaching) refers to the verbal instruction. "Amitābha" (Immeasurable Light) refers to the principle. Since these differ from other scriptures, there are thus three [categories].
If one examines each of these sutras individually against the word "sutra" (jīng), all three sutras are comprehensive in principle—that is, the Dharma-body;
in practice—that is, Prajñā; and in teaching—that is, Vimukti. These three are perfectly interfused and beyond conceptual discrimination; thus, they are called the Secret Treasury (*guhyagarbha*).
Therefore, by hearing the name of the title alone, one obtains immeasurable merit. The original title of this sutra is *Praise of the Inconceivable*.

The *Sūtra on the Merits Discussed by All Buddhas and Their Protective Mindfulness*, which was transmitted to China in two translations—the Tang translation being titled *The Sūtra of Praising the Pure Land and the Buddhas’ Acceptance*—now has its title omitted from the text.

Following the section on the Buddhas of the six directions, it simply states: "You sentient beings should believe in these [Buddhas]. This is because this sūtra correctly demonstrates the practice of holding the Name.
As for the method [of titling]: the holy name of Amitābha is something that all people delight to hear;

by using this to establish the title, many people will believe and accept it, thereby enabling it to be universally observed throughout the four seas and circulated without end. This is the skillful artistry of the translator. II. Discerning the Substance:
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that all Mahāyāna sūtras generally take the seal of the single true reality (*eka-tattva-lakṣaṇa-mudrā*) as their primary substance. That is to say—

This is the principle that is fully expressed. ○ Third, the *Sanming zongjing* (Scripture on the Three Clarifications of the Essential) states: "If there are those with faith, they should make a vow to be born in that land.
This is the essential core of this single scripture. ○ Fourth, the *Lun yong jing* (Scripture on the Application of the Treatise) states:
"One immediately attains rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, never regressing from unsurpassed bodhi, and departs from the suffering of birth and death."
The bliss of liberation is the power and function of this sutra. (5) Regarding the classification of its doctrinal characteristics: it is subsumed under the Vaipulya teachings of the Mahayana;

it clarifies the meaning of the two baskets and is included within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; and when divided into the gradual and sudden approaches, it belongs to the Sudden Teaching, because it causes ordinary beings not to regress from Bodhi.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty, by imperial decree.

Kumārajīva is here translated as "Child-Longevity" (Tóngshòu). He was a native of the country of Kučā. During the reign of the Later Qin Yao clan when they occupied Chang’an, he was honored as their National Teacher.
During the Hongshi era, he translated various sūtras and śāstras. The *Nanshan Gantong Zhuan* states:
He was a translator of the scriptures since the time of the seven Buddhas.
Thus it is said.
The commentary states: "Thus" refers to the essence of the Dharma as heard; the principle of the true mark (dharmatā) is the same throughout past and present.
It is said that it is correct to explain this as being "suchness" (tathatā) without distinction.
"I have heard":
"I" refers to Ānanda himself; Ānanda, when compiling the Dharma-piṭaka, spoke thus regarding this Dharma-gate.
"I heard this from the Buddha.
At one time— when the capacity [of the disciples] and the response [of the Buddha] were in harmony— the specific year, month, and day are not mentioned because the calendars of the two lands differ.
Therefore, "Buddha" is here translated as "The Awakened One.
His self-awakening distinguishes him from ordinary beings who lack awakening, and his awakening of others distinguishes him from those of the Two Vehicles who awaken only for themselves.
One who is awakened and whose awakening is complete, distinct from bodhisattvas who remain in the causal stage and honored among the multitude of sages, is therefore called a Buddha;
this refers to the Teacher Śākyamuni.
He was in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
Śrāvastī is correctly called Śrāvastī; this means "Hearing of Things," so named because its wealth and prosperity were heard of far and wide by all nations.
It was the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
In Sanskrit, *Jeta* means "Victorious in Battle"; it is the name of the crown prince of King Prasenajit. In Sanskrit, *Sudatta* means "Good Giver";
it is the name of the elder who was so called because he could generously bestow wealth upon the destitute of the kingdom, and thus was named "Giver of Orphans" (*Anāthapiṇḍada*).
He spread gold across the ground to purchase a garden from Jeta and established a monastery (*vihāra*) there, inviting the Buddha to preach the Dharma.
Because Jeta offered the trees, they are mentioned together.
He was with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
"Bhikṣu" is translated here as "mendicant" (qīsī): one who begs for food to sustain the body and begs for the Dharma to refine the mind; it is also called "Terrifier of Māra. Furthermore—
Regarding the "monks who have destroyed evil": *saṃgha* is fully explained as "the assembly in harmonious union.
There were one thousand two hundred and fifty people in total.
Among them, the three Kāśyapas had one thousand disciples, while Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana each had two hundred and fifty; these were the initial [members].
They have returned to the Buddha and constantly follow his assembly;
they are all great Arhats. The term "Arhat" contains three meanings:

first, "Worthy of Offerings," which refers to the fruit of the mendicant who serves as a field of merit for humans and devas; second, [the meaning of having destroyed the defilements]; third, [the meaning of being worthy of respect].

"Killing the thieves" means the exhaustion of afflictions (*kleśa*) and the total destruction of evil fruits; "the threefold non-arising" means not undergoing further existence, which is the fruit that terrifies Māra.
It is that which is known by all.
To hear the name and admire the virtue is called "knowledge" (jñā); to behold the form and reverently serve it is called "insight" (vijñā).

Elder Śāriputra—being of advanced age and eminent virtue, he is commonly titled Elder Śāriputra; this is translated as "Son of the Body" (Śarīraputra), because his mother’s physical appearance... [was so beautiful].
His features were upright and his eyes were like those of a śāri bird; combined with his mother’s name, he was called Śāriputra, foremost in wisdom.

Mahāmaudgalyāyana—this means "Great Mung Bean" (Maudgalya) as it was his clan name—and because his lineage was numerous, he was distinguished by the prefix "Great"; he was foremost in supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
1. Mahākāśyapa. This is translated as "Great Kauravya.
His ancestor was moved by a divine tortoise that emerged bearing a celestial chart; consequently, he took this as the name for his clan.
It is further said that the body-radiance of Kāśyapa was so brilliant and resplendent that it eclipsed all other lights.

During the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, he served as a master metalworker for a poor woman who offered him a gold bead to jointly construct a stūpa and an image; from that time onward, his body has always been golden in color.
Mahākātyāyana— here translated as "First in Ornamented Discourse"— and Mahākauṣṭhila.
This one is called Mahāmaudgalyāyana, named after his physical appearance; he was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra.
Revata means "Star"; his parents prayed to the stars for his birth, and thus he was given this name.
Cūḍapanthaka means "Successor on the Path" in this language.
His mother visited him while he was away; as she gave birth to him by the roadside, his disposition was dull and simple, and he could only recite half a verse, yet he attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Nanda was the younger brother of the Buddha; he is here called Shanhuānxǐ (Sukhābhirati). Ānanda—
This refers to Nanda, the son of King Śuklodana and the Buddha’s cousin. He was born on the day the Buddha attained enlightenment;
because the entire nation rejoiced, he was given the auspicious name Nanda, and he was foremost among those of great learning.

Rāhula is here translated as "Covering Obstruction," which is the original name of the Asura who is able to obstruct the sun and moon; because the Buddha was obstructed by him and he did not immediately leave the household life, it was adopted as his name.
Gavāmpati—this is translated as "Ox-Chewer," because in a previous life he was born as an ox; having finished eating, he would chew it over again, and thus he received this name. Piṇḍola Bharadvāja.
Pindola is translated here as "Immovable" (Acala); Pāṭhadra is translated as "Sharp Faculties" (Tīkṣṇendriya).
An alternative translation is Piṇḍula-bharadvāja. Kālodāyin.
This is called "Black Light" because its form is coarse and black.
Mahā-Kapphiṇa means "Mother of the Kṛttikā";
she was born after her mother prayed to the lunar mansion Kṛttikā.

Bakkula— here translated as "Good Appearance"— was so named because his physical form was upright and handsome; in the past, he offered a single *harītakī* fruit to the Saṃgha and thereby experienced the retribution of five lives free from death.
Aniruddha— translated here as "Free from Poverty"—
formerly offered millet porridge to a pratyekabuddha during a time of famine; for ninety-one kalpas,
his karmic retribution has been fully sufficient, and he is foremost in the divine eye.

These and other such great disciples are called "disciples" (弟) because their learning followed that of their teacher, and they are called "sons" (子) because their understanding was derived from the teacher; this is a summary of the preceding text.
Together with all the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
In the Sanskrit language, *bodhisattva* translates here as "enlightened sentient beings" (*jue youqing*). They are called "enlightened" because they share in the realization attained by the Buddhas;
they are called "sentient beings" because their ignorance is not yet exhausted. *Mahāsattva* translates here as "beings of the great path-mind."
Mañjuśrī Dharma Prince. Mañjuśrī is translated here as "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode), because he possesses the three subtle virtues identical to those realized by the Buddha;
he is also called the Bodhisattva Wondrous Auspiciousness (Miaojixiang). Having entered the correct stage of the Dharma, he is named a Dharma Prince.
The Bodhisattva Ajita—
here translated as "Incapable of Being Conquered"— is so named because he transcends both the partial and the small [vehicles].
The Bodhisattva Gandhahasti.
This is called "Unresting" because of being diligent and tireless;
it is the Bodhisattva Constantly Diligent,
who realizes that the nature of phenomena is eternally abiding and thus accomplishes unconditioned right effort.
Together with such great bodhisattvas as these—
who transcend the limited and the small— he distinguishes them by means of the term "great";
as well as Śakra-devānām-indra and others.
This refers to Śakra-devānām-indra, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,
together with an immeasurable assembly of devas—
namely, the Brahmā Kings of the Desire and Form Realms, the Four World-Protecting Kings, and so forth, as well as the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings.
Therefore, it is said that "the great assembly was together.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Elder Śāriputra.
"At that time" refers to the moment when he was about to preach the sutra; because Śāriputra possessed sharp faculties, the Buddha specifically addressed him.
He waited for him to inquire further.
From here, to the west, one passes through ten million *koṭi* of Buddha-lands.
One Buddha-land is equivalent to a great trichiliocosm. The *Ten Doubts Treatise* states that the West is ten million [yojanas] from here.
The mention of "hundreds of millions of Buddha-lands" is spoken merely in reference to the ordinary person's physical eye and the mental capacity of birth-and-death;
provided that sentient beings achieve pure karma, their state of meditative concentration at the moment of death is itself the mind for rebirth in a Pure Land.
Since the movement of thought is precisely the time of being born in the Pure Land, it is truly not far away.

There is a world named Sukhāvatī. In the Sanskrit language it is called *Sukhāvatī*, which is translated here as "Peaceful Nurturing" (*Ān-yǎng*), or "Pure Tranquility" (*Qīng-tài*), or "Ultimate Bliss" (*Jí-lè*). This last term signifies that which is most supreme.

All lands appear according to the perceptions of sentient beings, and there are four such types: first, the eternally quiescent; [the others being the land of constant illumination, the land of constant transformation, and the land of constant enjoyment].
First, the Land of Light, the dwelling place of the Buddhas who have attained the ultimate fruit; second, the Land of True Reward, the dwelling place of the Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body;
third, the Land of Expedient Means, the dwelling place of those of the Three Vehicles; and fourth, the Land of Common Residence, the dwelling place of the six classes of ordinary beings.

These are distinguished as pure or defiled based on the lightness or gravity of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*); because the five turbidities are heavy in this Sahā world, it includes the four evil destinies within its cycle.
Because the five turbidities are light there, those who turn their minds toward it and do not cease [their practice] will attain non-retrogression as humans or devas;
therefore, it is called "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī). To speak according to the ultimate principle, only the ultimate quiescent radiance is true Ultimate Bliss.
In that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha who currently dwells and expounds the Dharma. This Buddha possesses three bodies:

first, the *dharmatākāya* (dharma-nature body), which dwells in the Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhāsa-kṣetra*); since body and land are identical as one, it is called the "Secret Treasury" (*guhyakośa*).

Second, the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body), which dwells in the Land of True Reward (*sambhogakṣetra*). Third, the *nirmāṇakāya* (response-transformation body), which dwells in the two lower lands according to the nine grades [of rebirth].
The perceptions of those with different capacities vary; the teaching is spoken in the present to distinguish it from the past and future.
"Śāriputra, for what reason is that land called 'Ultimate Bliss'?
The preceding passage poses the question, and the following passage provides the general explanation, clarifying the adornments of the environment (*niśraya-vibhūṣaṇa*).
The sentient beings of that land are free from all suffering and experience only various joys; therefore, it is named "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī).
Regarding the phrase "free from all suffering," this means they are devoid of the various sufferings such as those of the three miserable realms and the eight difficulties.
It is called "Ultimate Bliss" in contrast to the extreme suffering of the Sahā world.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, the land of Ultimate Bliss has sevenfold railings—meaning crossbars and balustrades;
"lan" refers to the horizontal bars and "shun" to the vertical ones—which adorn jeweled trees and surround clusters of flowers.
Seven layers of jeweled nets cover it,
their radiant colors shimmering as they hang down all around in a magnificent and ornate display.
There are also seven rows of trees.
The *Contemplation Sūtra* states: "Each tree is eight thousand yojanas high, and its flowers and leaves made of the seven treasures are fully complete.
All are surrounded on all sides by the four precious substances; therefore, that land is named 'Ultimate Bliss' (Sukhāvatī)."
The four treasures are gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, in the land of Ultimate Bliss there are ponds made of the seven treasures.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "The waters of these two ponds are composed of the seven treasures; those treasures are soft and supple, arising from the King of Wish-fulfilling Jewels."
It is filled with water possessing eight virtues. The Chinese translation states:
first, it is clear and pure; second, it is cool and refreshing; third, it is sweet; fourth, it is light and soft; fifth, it is moistening; sixth...
Seventh, it brings peace and harmony; eighth, it eliminates hunger and thirst and nurtures the sense faculties.
The bottom of the pond is entirely covered with golden sand.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "The channels are made of gold, and beneath these channels, the riverbed is composed of various colored diamond sands."
The stairways on its four sides are composed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and *sphatika*.
"Lapis lazuli" (*vaiḍūrya*) is translated here as "not far away," for this jewel is found not far from the city of Vārāṇasī, and thus it is named accordingly.
"*Sphatika*" is translated as "water-jade."

The lotuses in the pond are as large as chariot wheels.

Regarding the size of a chariot wheel, Master Lingzhi said it is difficult to establish a fixed standard; however, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that the thousand-spoked wheel of a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin) has a circumference of fifteen li.
The blue [lotuses] have blue light; the yellow, yellow light; the red, red light; and the white, white light—subtle, wondrous, fragrant, and pure.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states that within each pond there are sixty billion lotus flowers made of the seven treasures; thus they do not merely possess four colors.
Furthermore, each lotus flower is perfectly round and twelve yojanas in diameter; it is not merely the size of a chariot wheel.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "The lotuses in the pond may be one yojana in size, or even up to a hundred thousand yojanas.
This shows that what is perceived differs according to the capacity of the individual.
Śāriputra, the Land of Ultimate Bliss is thus adorned with such perfected merits and splendors.
The adornments of the Buddha-land are all accomplished through Amitābha’s cultivation of bodhisattva practices and vows over many kalpas.
Regarding the citations in the text: the "Great Sūtra" refers to the two-fascicle *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, which extensively discusses the pure realm;
the "Contemplation Sūtra" refers to the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra*, which extensively clarifies the aspects of practice; and the present sūtra provides a concise exposition, as is commonly known.
The term "small version" (*xiǎoběn*) refers to it in contrast to the "large version" (*dàběn*).
Furthermore, Śāriputra, in that buddha-land, celestial music is constantly performed.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "Immeasurable devas perform celestial music," and there are musical instruments suspended in the void.
It is like a celestial jewel banner that resounds spontaneously without being struck; as the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states, there are also ten thousand kinds of natural musical performances.
Furthermore, these musical sounds are none other than the sound of the Dharma—clear, lofty, plaintive, resonant, subtle, and elegant—surpassing all other sounds and beyond their reach.
The ground is made of gold.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states that the ground is of lapis lazuli, with golden cords interspersed and interwoven, and further demarcated by the seven treasures;
what is here called "gold" refers merely to the adornment of the surface of the ground.
Six times throughout the day and night, it rains celestial *māndārava* flowers.

*Māndārava* is translated here as "white flower" (*pāṇḍarapuṣpa*) or "pleasing" (*manojña*). However, because that land is constantly illuminated by its own radiance rather than by the sun and moon, there is no distinction between day and night;
according to the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, the opening of the lotuses and the singing of the birds mark the dawn.
Birds gather there to roost at night, and there are no four seasons—spring, autumn, winter, or summer; it is neither cold nor hot, but always temperate and harmonious.
The sentient beings of that land always, at the clear dawn, each take a robe-sack to gather various wonderful flowers.
*Yījì* (衣裓) refers to the lapel of a robe; Paramārtha states it is a vessel for holding flowers used in foreign lands.
[The text says he] made offerings to ten trillion Buddhas in other directions.

The *Daben* (大本, Mahāvaipulya) version states that, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, he traveled in the space of a single meal to immeasurable worlds in the ten directions to pay his respects.
He reverently made offerings to the Buddhas.
Then, at the time for eating, he returned to his own land to eat, drink, and practice walking meditation.
"The time for eating" refers to the period before noon. The *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra] states: "If one wishes to eat, bowls and vessels made of the seven precious gems appear spontaneously."

Before them, food and drink of a hundred flavors spontaneously overflow; upon seeing their colors and smelling their fragrances, they are naturally satiated, their bodies and minds becoming supple and free from any attachment to taste.
Once they have finished eating, the food vanishes; when the time comes again, it reappears.
Śāriputra, the land of Sukhāvatī is adorned with such meritorious accomplishments.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, that land always has various wonderful birds of diverse colors.
The rare birds of the Pure Land differ from the winged species of the Sahā world; thus they are described as "wondrous.
The Tathāgata spoke in accordance with worldly conventions, and the translators rendered them by drawing analogies from familiar species:
white cranes, peacocks, and parrots.
These three can be understood. Śāriputra;
"Śāri" here means "spring parrot" or "śālika crane."
The kalaviṅka— translated here as the "Bird of Wondrous Sound"— while still within its shell, its voice already surpasses that of all other birds.
Then there is the jīvañjīvaka bird.
Two heads on one body, they share the same consciousness but differ in their dharmas; as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says, they are called "life-and-life" (*jīvajīvaka*) birds.
These various birds, throughout the six periods of day and night, produce harmonious and elegant sounds.
Those sounds expound and clarify the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).

1. The faculty of faith, 2. the faculty of diligence, 3. the faculty of mindfulness, 4. the faculty of concentration, and 5. the faculty of wisdom are called "faculties" (*indriya*) because they are able to give rise to the Noble Path.
The five powers (*bala*).
The same faculties (*indriya*) are called "powers" (*bala*) because they are capable of dispelling karmic obstacles.
The seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*):

*bodhi* here refers to "awakening," and the term "factors" (*aṅga*) is also translated as "limbs. First, the factor of mindfulness of awakening; second, the factor of discernment of phenomena. Third...

The awakening factor of diligence (vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga), the fifth awakening factor of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga), the sixth awakening factor of tranquility (praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga), the seventh awakening factor of concentration (samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga), and the eighth awakening factor of equanimity (upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga).

Regarding the Noble Eightfold Path, various sūtras state it as follows: first, right view (samyagdṛṣṭi); second, right intention (samyaksaṃkalpa); third, right speech (samyagvāc); fourth, right [action]...
The five [factors of] karma, right livelihood as the sixth, right effort as the seventh, right mindfulness as the eighth, and right concentration—

such dharmas as these constitute the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharmas). [This list] is incomplete because it lacks the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, and the three categories [of the noble truths].
Regarding phenomena such as clouds:
when the sentient beings of that land hear this sound, they all recollect the Buddha, recollect the Dharma, and recollect the Saṃgha.孤山 (Gushan) said:

"Recollecting the Buddha is like [recollecting] a king of physicians; recollecting the Dharma is like [recollecting] excellent medicine; and recollecting the Saṃgha is like [recollecting] a caregiver."

When these three conditions are complete, the disease of affliction can be cured. Furthermore, if one contemplates that one’s own mind is quiescent yet constantly luminous, then all phenomena will appear with brilliant clarity;
this is called mindfulness of the Buddha. Being luminous yet constantly quiescent, such that not a single phenomenon can be named, is called mindfulness of the Dharma.
This non-duality of quiescence and luminosity—being present yet extinguished—is called mindfulness of the Sangha. These constitute the Three Jewels as a single essence. —Lingzhi (Yuanzhao)
It is said that in this realm, the minds of beings are defiled and constantly contemplate the five desires, whereas in that land, the minds are pure and single-mindedly mindful of the Triple Gem;
the relative elevation and decline of these two lands can be seen from this.
Śāriputra, do not say that these birds are truly born as a result of their karmic retribution for sins.
How can there be such things in a Pure Land, which is summoned by the meritorious karma of beings, when it is drawn from the sinful karma of birds and beasts in a defiled world?
Why is this so? Because in that Buddha-land, there are no three evil realms.
As stated in the original vow of the Bhikṣu Dharmākara: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or [animals] within my land..."
Śāriputra, that Buddha-land does not even have the name of the three evil realms, let alone their actual existence.
That land is so pure that it lacks even the names of the three evil realms, much less the beings born there as a result of karmic retribution for their sins.
Are these real entities?
These various birds are all transformations produced by Amitābha Buddha, intended to cause the sound of the Dharma to flow forth.
The *Contemplation Sūtra* says: "The King of Wish-Fulfilling Jewels surges forth with subtle and wondrous golden light; that light transforms into..."

Lingzhi said: "One should know that these birds of a hundred jewel-like colors, singing together with harmonious and elegant tones, are the supernatural power of the Tathāgata intended to cause the sound of the Dharma to resound; one must understand that they do not arise as a retribution for past transgressions."
Śāriputra, when a gentle breeze stirs the rows of jewel trees and the jeweled nets in that Buddha-land, they produce a subtle and wondrous sound,
like the simultaneous playing of hundreds of thousands of kinds of music. Those who hear this sound naturally give rise to thoughts of mindfulness of the Buddha,
mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Saṅgha.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "A gentle breeze stirs, blowing through the various jeweled trees and producing immeasurable sounds of the wondrous Dharma.
These sounds spread throughout all Buddha-lands; those who hear them attain the profound *dharmakṣānti*. Furthermore, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* says:
"The water from the *maṇi* jewels flows among the flowers, expounding the [truths of] suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, as well as the various *pāramitās*."
Luo Mi’s Gushan says: "Though jeweled towers and golden ponds provide visual delights, they do not consist of colors that lead to delusion or dissipation;

rather, one can thereby realize that there is only mind and no external objects. Though the sound of wind in the trees and the cries of birds provide auditory pleasures, they do not consist of discordant or jarring tones;
rather, one can thereby maintain mindfulness of the Three Jewels as one's refuge."
Śāriputra, that buddha-field of that Buddha is thus adorned with such meritorious qualities.
Śāriputra, what do you think? For what reason is that Buddha named Amitābha?
Having examined whether they have understood, he next provides an explanation to clarify it:
"Śāriputra, that Buddha’s light is immeasurable; it illuminates the lands of the ten directions without obstruction.
For this reason, he is named Amitābha."
The *Mahāvaipulya* Sūtra states: "The majestic virtue and radiant light of Amitābha Buddha are most honored and supreme;

the lights of all other Buddhas cannot equal them. The *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* states: "He shines universally throughout the ten directions, embracing and never abandoning those sentient beings who recite his name.
Someone asked: "If his radiance is immeasurable, why do I not see it? The answer is: "When the bright sun adorns the heavens, the blind man does not behold it."
This is the fault of the blind; sentient beings have such heavy obstructions that they are as if situated beneath a covered bowl—it is not that the sunlight does not shine upon them.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, the lifespan of that Buddha and that of his people shall be immeasurable and boundless asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Therefore, he is named Amitābha.
"A-saṃkhyeya" is translated here as "innumerable. The *Mūla* [Sutra] states: "The lifespan of that Buddha cannot be measured or calculated.
Suppose all sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions were to become Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and they were to exhaust their intellectual powers for a hundred..."
Even if one were to calculate together for a thousand kalpas, one could not exhaustively fathom this treasury of Dharma. His original vow states:
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the lifespan of the humans and devas in my land should be limited and measurable, and if it were otherwise than this, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
"Śāriputra, since Amitābha Buddha attained Buddhahood, ten kalpas have now passed.
The preceding general statement, "He is currently preaching the Dharma," indicates the number of kalpas since he became a Buddha.
The *Mahāvaipulya* version states, "Since attaining Buddhahood, a total of ten kalpas have elapsed," while the Tang translation says, "Ten great kalpas have passed"; both mean the same thing.
The doctrine that [the Buddha] appears for a single period to respond to the capacities of beings is indeed superior;
yet, since the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) extends through the three periods of time and fills the ten directions without limit, how could its duration be measured by the calculation of kalpas?
Furthermore, Śāriputra, that Buddha has immeasurable and boundless śrāvaka disciples, all of whom are arhats, beyond what can be known by calculation.

They are called "śrāvakas" because they hear the sound of the teaching on the Four Noble Truths and thereby awaken to the Path; they are all arhats, which distinguishes them from those mentioned previously.

Regarding the three fruits, it is not said that the *pratyekabuddhas* are included within the number of *śrāvakas*. In Vasubandhu’s commentary (*Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*), it is stated that those of the two vehicles’ lineage do not produce [the Buddha-nature];

however, because it is now said that they turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle, they are able to produce it. Because they were habituated to the Small Vehicle, they provisionally realize the two vehicles, but before long they will realize the Great.
It is the same for all bodhisattvas and sentient beings.

It is not only the śrāvakas who are immeasurable; bodhisattvas are likewise immeasurable. While the śrāvaka is common to both teachings of the Two Vehicles, the bodhisattva is common to the four teachings, though the primary intent lies in the Perfect [Teaching].
Śāriputra, that buddha-land is adorned with such meritorious qualities;
this ocean-like assembly of beings, which is joyful, supreme, and immeasurable, is all accomplished through the power of Amitābha’s vows.
Śāriputra, those born in the land of Sukhāvatī are all *avaivartika*. *Avaivartika* here means "non-retrogressive.

As the subsequent text states that they are all non-retrogressive regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one knows that although those born in that land may be ordinary beings of the lowest grade, they will proceed directly to the attainment of Buddhahood without further regression.
The *Dabon* (Mahāvaipulya) states: "All sentient beings who are born in that land are fully endowed with the thirty-two marks;
their faculties are sharp and keen, and they shall not fall into the evil realms until they attain Buddhahood. They possess sovereign supernormal powers and constant knowledge of past lives.
In this world, there are sixty-seven billion non-retrogressive bodhisattvas who will be reborn in that land."

Among them, there are many who are in their last birth before Buddhahood; their number is so vast that it cannot be known by calculation, but can only be described as being for immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) kalpas.

"One-life-to-enlightenment" (*ekajātipratibaddha*) refers to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), also called the "final body" (*paścima-deha*), meaning that one will become a Buddha after only one more birth;
Maitreya in this land is an example of this. In that land, it is Avalokiteśvara who is next to succeed to Buddhahood, and Śrīkṣetra (Potuoshizhi) who will succeed Avalokiteśvara.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The bodhisattvas in that land all attain ultimate perfection."

Those who are in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*)—except for those who, out of their original vow, adorn themselves with the armor of great resolve for the sake of sentient beings—are so numerous that they cannot be calculated; therefore, they are called *asaṃkhyeya*.
Śāriputra, those sentient beings who hear this should make a vow, vowing to be born in that land.
A vow can guide one’s practice, just as a cow pulling a cart requires a driver to reach its destination; the purification of a Buddha-land is accomplished through the guidance of a vow.
As the *Tianqin lun* (Vasubandhu’s Treatise) states: "The roots of goodness cultivated by a Bodhisattva are not for their own sake..."
Because he desires to uproot the suffering of all sentient beings, he gathers them in to be born together with him in that land. The Four Clarities state:
"It is only because their merit from the precepts is not refined and they lack the vow for rebirth there, that they remain in this defiled land.

One must fear that although one hears the Dharma and enters the truth here, in the Sahā world Buddhas do not always appear; the sensory environments are coarse and powerful, making it truly a perilous place where many fall back."

Because [the roots of goodness] have been lost, one must externally perform ritual repentance and internally apply diligent contemplation of the principle, while adding vows and strict self-restraint, so that one may swiftly realize non-arising in the Jewel Land. Why is this?
It is because one has attained the opportunity to assemble together with such superior and virtuous people in a single place.
"The various superior and virtuous persons" refers to the aforementioned śrāvakas and bodhisattvas who are in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*). Cijue said:
"In the Sahā world, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta merely look up to their illustrious names; in the Sukhāvatī world, those two superior persons personally act as one's supreme friends.
Just as a person who has been smeared with incense has the fragrance of that incense upon their body, [the inhabitants of Sukhāvatī] do not regress from their bodhi."
Because they are identical to what the Buddha has realized—namely, the Dharma-nature body and the eternally quiescent light—it is said that they "assemble together in one place.
Śāriputra, one cannot be born in that land through the causes and conditions of meager roots of goodness or merit.
Lingzhi said: To manifest the superiority of the merit of holding the name, one must first disparage other blessings as being minor roots of goodness.

Whether it be giving, precepts, meditation, recitation, or any other meritorious activity, if they lack right faith and the aspiration for dedication, they are all minor roots of goodness and not causes for rebirth.
Only by relying on this sutra to single-mindedly hold the name and vow for rebirth can they be called "abundant roots of goodness."
The roots are the good roots; clarity and right practice refer to upholding the Name with single-mindedness and without distraction.
Regarding merit as auxiliary practice, the *Contemplation Sūtra* states: "Those who wish to be born in that land should cultivate the three types of merit:

first, filially supporting one's parents, serving teachers and elders, possessing a compassionate heart and refraining from killing, and practicing the ten virtuous deeds; second, receiving and upholding the Three Refuges..."
To be fully endowed with the various precepts and not violate dignified conduct; third, to give rise to the bodhicitta, have deep faith in cause and effect,
recite and study the Mahāyāna, and encourage others to practice— these three matters are called pure karma, and they are all auxiliary practices for rebirth [in the Pure Land].
Śāriputra, if there are good men or good women who, upon hearing the teaching of Amitābha Buddha, grasp and maintain his name—Guishan says:
"Grasping" means to take up and receive; "maintaining" means to sustain and hold. Because of the power of faith, one takes it up and receives it within the mind and mindfulness.
By the power [of that practice], one maintains it without forgetting;
whether for one day, two days, three days, four days, five days, six days, or seven days,
one remains single-mindedly without distraction.

"Young man" is an indefinite term. Those of sharp faculties may achieve success in a single day or a single thought-moment; those of dull faculties may require up to seven days for the practice to be perfected.
Even if one subsequently breaks the precepts, it is certain to become a cause for rebirth. Regarding "single-mindedness without distraction," there is both the substantial and the principled.
Substantial single-mindedness means that the practitioner binds their attention and recollects the physical marks, features, and radiant light of Amitābha Buddha. As for... [text ends]

The uninterrupted state of non-distracted attention is called "single-mindedness in practice. As for single-mindedness: one thoroughly realizes that both the mind capable of recollecting and the Buddha who is recollected are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Although they are fundamentally empty and quiescent, their resonance and response intersect like reflections in a mirror, the moon in water, or the moon's reflection in water;
they manifest and benefit spontaneously, yet are empty in their very locus. This entire reality is simultaneously both empty and provisional, transcending the two extremes.
When one attains the Middle Way, the three truths do not exist as separate entities; they are perfectly interfused, transcending thought and discourse. This is called "one mind in principle.
However, one must thoroughly realize that the Dharma-realm is solely mind and that there is no object outside of mind.

The physical marks and signs of Amitābha are originally one's own mind, and the distance of ten million *yojanas* does not exceed the present moment. Because all phenomena are inherently possessed within one's nature, they are not obtained from without. Furthermore...
Furthermore, one should know that Amitābha has already realized the ultimate, primary truth;

with a single invocation of his auspicious name, his myriad virtues are simultaneously manifested, erasing the sins of kalpas as numerous as motes of dust and bestowing blessings equal to the void. How much more so for those who practice for one day up to seven days!

This is entirely due to the fundamental vows of Dharmākara: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the sentient beings of the ten directions should, with a sincere heart, believe and rejoice, desiring to be born..."

"If even ten recitations of my name should not arise in one's mind, may I not attain perfect enlightenment"—having received this immeasurable merit of upholding the Name through the power of that Buddha’s vows during his causal stage and his radiance upon his fruition, one will certainly see the Buddha at the moment of death;
of this there is no doubt. (In the *Lingzhi shu*, citing the Shiyang stone edition, [the phrase] "with single-mindedness and without distraction" appears below [this passage]).
Some say that by single-mindedly upholding the Name, the fact that all transgressions are extinguished through this recitation constitutes a cause and condition for many roots of goodness and merit.
I suspect that the present edition has suffered from errors and omissions during its transmission, as the stone-script edition was written by people of the Six Dynasties period.
Furthermore, our Amitābha Buddha welcomes sentient beings with His Name; when it is heard by the ear and recited by the mouth, His boundless holy virtues are thereby embraced.
The conscious mind shall forever become the seed of Buddhahood; one will instantly eliminate the heavy sins of billions of kalpas and attain realization of unsurpassed Bodhi.
One may truly know that this is not due to meager roots of goodness, but is indeed said to be the result of manifold merit.
At the time when such a person approaches the end of their life, Amitābha Buddha and the assembly of holy beings will appear before them.

Lingzhi remarked that there are many ways in which the holy assembly may appear; whether they be the true Buddha, an emanation Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, or Mahāsthāmaprāpta, these matters depend on one's spiritual rank and are detailed in the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*. Furthermore, some claim that seeing the Buddha at the moment of death is actually the work of a māra.
Some say that because the karma of one’s own mind manifests reality, there is no other Buddha who comes or goes;

this is a grave error, for it stems from ignorance of the fact that the living being and the Buddha are of one essence and that their response and resonance intersect. To obstruct oneself and others in this way is no small transgression.
As the *Primal Vow of Dharmakara* states: "If sentient beings, having made a vow to be born in my land, should at the time of their death not be surrounded by a great assembly..."
I shall not attain perfect enlightenment before manifesting myself before that person.
At the time of this person's death, their mind shall not be inverted;
sustained by the power of Amitābha’s vows, their mind shall not be shaken by the habitual攀緣 (pān-yuán) of deluded thoughts.
Because right mindfulness is present, it is said that the mind is not inverted;
one will immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.

Due to this prior recitation of the Buddha's name, transgressions are extinguished and hindrances are removed; pure karma internally perfumes the mind while the compassionate light externally gathers one in, so that one leaves suffering behind and attains liberation.
"To rejoice for even a single kṣaṇa.
Śāriputra, it is because I see such benefits that I say this: if there are sentient beings who hear this teaching, they should make a vow to be born in that land."
The merit of pure karma is the most essential; for this reason, the Tathāgata has exhorted and encouraged [beings] repeatedly.
Śāriputra, just as I now praise the inconceivable merit of Amitābha Buddha, so too [should you].

The preceding section reiterates the praise of the merits of the adornments of the environment and its inhabitants (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*), as well as the vows, practices, and benefits, which are immeasurable;
this serves as an analogy for the Buddhas of the six directions, all of whom are likewise praised in this manner to encourage the arising of faith.

The Chinese translation includes the ten directions, whereas this version mentions only the six, merely omitting the four intermediate points. According to the *Shu* (Commentary) by Gushan, the following section belongs to the *Pravartana* (Circulation). Now...
This refers to the praise by all Buddhas; it is the title of this sutra and its essential purport, which together converge upon the correct teaching.
To the east there is also the Buddha Akṣobhya, which here is translated as "Immovable";
his *dharmakāya* is eternally abiding because it is free from transition or change.
Sumeru-lakṣaṇa Buddha.

"Sumeru" is translated here as "Wondrously High. His marks are like those [of Sumeru]: "wondrous" signifies the perfect fusion of the three virtues (*triguṇa*), and "high" signifies transcending the stage of causes.
Mahāmeru Buddha. The Buddha’s virtues are as lofty and vast as Mount Sumeru, surpassing all other mountains.
Sumeruprabha Buddha.
His radiance is like Mount Sumeru, eclipsing all other mountains.
Buddha Wondrous Sound:
His voice is exquisite and beautiful; he preaches the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.
There were as many such Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.
The Ganges, also known as the Gaṅgā, flows beside the Anavatapta Lake in India;
it is forty *li* wide, and its sands are so fine that they flow along with the water—hence the expression is used to signify their great number.
In each of their respective lands, they extend their broad and long tongues, completely covering the trichiliocosm.
They extend their broad and long tongues to manifest that they are free from falsehood; because for immeasurable kalpas their speech has been free from the four faults, they have elicited this mark.
As the *Trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātukośa-gāthā* says: "The four great continents, the sun and moon, and Mount Sumeru..."
One thousand realms of the desire heavens and the Brahma worlds are called a small chiliocosm; one thousand times this small chiliocosm is termed a medium chiliocosm;

and one thousand times this medium chiliocosm is a great trichiliocosm, all of which undergo formation and destruction simultaneously. That is to say, ten thousand sets of four continents constitute a single Buddha-field in total.
"I speak these truthful words; you sentient beings should believe them, for they are certainly not false.
Thus he speaks of truthfulness. The Buddhas of the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, with one voice and in unison, proclaim this Dharma-gate to inspire deep faith.

this is the Sutra of Principle, which concerns the inherently existing nature and virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*). These three sutras are the secret treasury of the three virtues, perfectly encompassing all as one.
When fully unfolded, it encompasses the entire Dharma-realm; when rolled up, it is contained within a single sutra.

The *kalpa-kaṣāya* (Aeon-turbidity). In Sanskrit, *kalpa* means "time-period. It refers to the period when human lifespan decreases from twenty thousand years; at that time, one enters the *kalpa-kaṣāya*.
The four turbidities (*catur-kaṣāya*) intensify and gather during this time, with malice increasing until weapons of war arise and greed and desire flourish.
Famine intensifies, ignorance and darkness arise, diseases increase, and the three calamities emerge;
consequently, afflictions flourish twofold, false views blaze ever more fiercely, and the various turbidities converge like waters rushing toward a dark abyss.

The turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*) refers to the five dull fetters— greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt— as well as the one hundred and eight afflictions and so forth. The turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).

As for the term "joy," its meaning encompasses both the profound and the shallow: it may refer to obtaining the benefit of joy, or to realizing the principle and entering the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

*A Brief Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra* (End).

Although the texts of the Great Canon spoken by our Buddha, the Sage, differ in their respective origins, they all serve nothing other than to transform people toward goodness and lead them into the realm of the Buddha.

Yet, among the seven types of Mahāyāna teachings, the particular emphasis placed on the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is intended to cause sentient beings to fix their minds upon a single point, so that pure karma may be easily accomplished. If...

The *Smaller Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* is one of the seven sutras that exclusively praise [Amitābha]. First, it extensively praises the supreme majesty of the two types of retribution—the environment and its inhabitants;
next, it cites the fact that this is identical to the sincere and non-deceptive protection and mindfulness of all Buddhas;

and finally, it exhorts the practice of vows to ensure rebirth in the Pure Land. Thus, its language is concise while its principles are clear, and its expressions are brief while its matters are complete. Is this not so?
However, while there are many people among the world’s readers of this work, those who truly understand it are few.

After Master Qizong had devoted his heart to the practice of pure karma (*śukla-karma*), he searched through and extracted the essential phrases from the patriarchal inquiries to provide an exposition of this text, titling it the *Lüejiè* (Brief Commentary). By grasping the collar and lifting the framework, he ensured that all its essentials were attained;

thus, upon opening the scroll, one may attain a clear, refreshing understanding, and following the text, interpretations arise, which, when formed into contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), lead to a wondrous realization of the ultimate truth (*tathatā*).
The nature of the Pure Land is Amitābha; it does not require seeking elsewhere, but is attained spontaneously through a single undistracted mind.
How could this not be of great benefit to one's pure conduct? Therefore, I have composed this preface at the end.
